slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Open by making the chapter question operational rather than historical. The goal is not to replace affine geometry, but to add exactly the missing boundary data that lets parallel directions become ordinary projective incidences. Keep returning to the three verbs on the slide: complete the space, read incidence at infinity, and choose infinity to simplify a theorem.

slides.label: Three Completion Models
slides.notes: The source span compares several constructions of the same completion. Present them as tools with different costs. Coordinates make examples fast, vectorization gives a picture of the affine slice and boundary slice, and the intrinsic projective space explains why the construction does not depend on arbitrary coordinate choices. Students should see one object through three lenses.

slides.label: Completion Definition
slides.notes: Emphasize the category mistake the slide is designed to prevent. An ideal point is not a remote finite point reached after traveling a long time. It is the direction class of all finite lines with a common direction. The notebook artifact helps because the finite chart and boundary are visually distinct, so students can point to which part stores positions and which part stores directions.

slides.label: Affine Chart From Projective Space
slides.notes: This is the converse direction of the relationship. A projective space does not come with a preferred affine chart until a hyperplane is singled out as infinity. Once that choice is made, ratios with the last coordinate recover affine coordinates. The phrase move the boundary should mean changing the affine interpretation while the underlying projective incidence structure remains unchanged.

slides.label: Affine Maps Extend
slides.notes: Use the block matrix as the algebraic hinge of the lecture. The lower row says that the chosen hyperplane at infinity is preserved. The translation vector changes finite positions, but it has no effect on ideal points because ideal points only remember direction. Conversely, when a projective transformation respects the chosen boundary, its finite chart action must be affine.

slides.label: Projective Line Laboratory
slides.notes: The projective line is a compact laboratory for the whole chapter. The formula shows exactly when a finite value becomes infinite: the denominator vanishes. It also shows when infinity stays fixed. This prepares students for the later technique of choosing a projective change of coordinates so that an inconvenient finite object becomes part of the boundary.

slides.label: Parallel Lines
slides.notes: This is the chapter's most teachable slogan, but it should be stated precisely. Parallel affine lines do not secretly cross inside the affine chart. Their completed projective lines intersect on the boundary, at the ideal point determined by their common direction. The notebook figure is useful because it separates the visible finite lines from the marked shared boundary point.

slides.label: Subspace Closure
slides.notes: Move from lines to arbitrary affine subspaces. The closure formula is the main idea: add the projectivized direction space. If two subspaces are parallel, their finite locations differ but their direction spaces agree, so their ideal parts agree. If one direction space sits inside another, that inclusion is visible as incidence inside the boundary hyperplane.

slides.label: Boundary Dictionary
slides.notes: This slide slows the lecture down into a usable dictionary. The point of the chapter is not merely that projective geometry is larger. It is that certain affine questions become cleaner because the missing cases are moved into a boundary where ordinary incidence language applies. The warning is important because projective drawings can make nonparallel lines appear visually suggestive.

slides.label: Sending To Infinity
slides.notes: Introduce sending to infinity as a disciplined change of chart, not as a mystical operation. A projective transformation preserves the incidence facts being proved. What changes is the affine interpretation after we choose a new boundary. This is why the same theorem can have a projective version and several affine shadows depending on which object has been placed at infinity.

slides.label: Pappus Shadow
slides.notes: The source span uses Pappus as an application of sending objects to infinity. Keep the statement qualitative here: the projective theorem gives collinearity of three constructed intersection points. If that collinearity line is chosen as the new boundary, the affine interpretation says the corresponding finite lines have become parallel. The power is that one projective proof controls many affine-looking cases.

slides.label: Desargues Shadow
slides.notes: Desargues is useful because it has two visible features that can be sent to infinity: the center of perspectivity and the axis of side intersections. The projective theorem treats them uniformly as incidence data. The affine reader sees different-looking theorems depending on which feature is placed on the boundary. This reinforces that affine special cases are shadows of one projective configuration.

slides.label: Fundamental Theorem
slides.notes: Do not try to prove the full fundamental theorem on the slide. Instead, show the reduction strategy. A hyperplane choice creates an affine chart. On that chart, collinearity preservation becomes an affine theorem about semilinear maps. Once the semilinear map is found, projectivizing it gives the projective transformation. This is another instance of choosing a boundary to make the problem accessible.

slides.label: Computational Checks
slides.notes: Connect the lecture deck back to the notebook's quality contract. The figures are not decoration: each one has an inspection target and a small certificate. The checks are modest, but they support the teaching habit that visual output should be tied to an invariant or diagnostic. Here the invariant language is completion, shared ideal direction, and nonblank generated evidence.

slides.label: Exercise And Recap
slides.notes: Close with a concrete computation students can do immediately. The slope determines the ideal point, while the intercept only moves the finite representative. A vertical line has direction vector zero one, so its ideal point is zero one zero. The recap should leave students with a workflow: complete the affine picture, inspect the boundary, then choose a chart that makes the desired incidence visible.
